title: Lightning Hit a Moon Rocket 36 Seconds After Launch. Then Hit It Again

scenes.text: Lightning hit a Moon rocket 36 seconds after launch. Then again.
November 1969. Apollo 12 climbs into a rain cloud, three astronauts on top.
At 36 seconds, a bolt runs down the rocket to the ground. At 52 seconds, a second strike.
Every warning light comes on. The fuel cells drop offline.
scenes.keywords: spacecraft cockpit warning lights control panel

scenes.text: A 26-year-old engineer says: try S C E to auxiliary. One switch. The data comes back.
The rocket had made its own lightning. Ten days later, they walked on the Moon.

description:
On 14 November 1969, Apollo 12 was struck by lightning twice during launch, at 36.5 seconds and 52 seconds after liftoff.
The strikes knocked all three fuel cells offline and scrambled the navigation platform. Flight controller John Aaron's call, SCE to AUX, restored the telemetry and let the crew reset the fuel cells. A later study found the cloud was too weak to make lightning by itself: the rocket and its hot exhaust plume triggered the strikes.
Would you have pressed on to the Moon after that launch? Comment below.
first_comment: The engineer who made the call, John Aaron, was 26 years old. He only knew the fix because he had seen the same weird telemetry pattern in a test a year earlier. Would you have trusted a switch nobody had heard of?
